title: Musk says Terrafab chip factory could outperform rivals despite challenges
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
Investing.com -- Elon Musk said his companies could eventually manufacture semiconductors more efficiently than industry rivals, although he acknowledged that mastering chip production could take several years.
Speaking via livestream at the X Takeover event outside Tesla’s Austin gigafactory on Saturday, Musk said his companies’ experience developing customised manufacturing equipment could provide an advantage in semiconductor production.
Musk acknowledged that chipmaking remains one of the world’s most technically demanding industries and that he currently lacks direct expertise in semiconductor manufacturing.
He said his companies could nevertheless develop superior production methods, although achieving that goal might take several years.
The comments come as Musk prepares to develop Terrafab, a semiconductor manufacturing facility in Grimes, Texas, through a joint venture involving Tesla (NASDAQ), SpaceX (NASDAQ) and Intel (NASDAQ).
The project carries an initial investment exceeding $15 billion and is expected to create approximately 3,000 jobs.
Texas authorities have approved a $30 million grant through the Texas Enterprise Fund to support the development.
The planned facility will cover approximately 100 million square feet across a roughly 3,000-acre footprint, with construction taking place in phases.
SpaceX currently controls more than 13,000 acres in the surrounding area.
The semiconductor initiative forms part of Musk’s broader push to expand manufacturing capacity across his companies, including infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence and autonomous technologies.
Tesla separately reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter vehicle deliveries on Friday, shipping 486,532 vehicles worldwide against analysts’ average forecast of 463,761.
The electric vehicle manufacturer plans to spend more than $25 billion this year expanding factory operations and developing its robotaxi business.
Tesla has also secured $30 billion in new loans and credit facilities to support its growth plans.
The Terrafab project would represent a major expansion into semiconductor manufacturing, an industry requiring substantial capital investment and specialised technical expertise.

title: Foreign investors flee South Korean stocks as AI boom loses steam
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
Investing.com -- South Korean stocks are struggling to attract buyers as enthusiasm for artificial intelligence-related investments fades, triggering heavy foreign outflows and a sharp decline in trading activity.
Trading turnover in South Korea’s $4.3 trillion equity market has plunged 70% from its late-May peak, while the benchmark Kospi has fallen 22% in the second half of 2026, according to Bloomberg.
The reversal follows a first-half rally that made the Kospi the world’s best-performing major equity benchmark, driven largely by demand for AI memory chips.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which together account for more than half the index’s weighting, have become a source of vulnerability as investors question whether the semiconductor boom can continue.
Foreign investors have withdrawn $131 billion from Korean equities this year, the largest outflow among major Asian markets, according to exchange data compiled by Bloomberg.
Concerns over demand were evident when Samsung shares declined Thursday despite the company reporting a nearly ninefold increase in quarterly operating profit.
Market support from corporate share repurchases is also weakening. Samsung and SK Hynix are approaching completion of combined buyback programmes worth 55 trillion won ($41 billion).
Retail participation has similarly declined following July’s selloff.
Outstanding margin loans have fallen to approximately 33 trillion won from a June peak of 38.6 trillion won, while brokerage deposits have dropped to around 100 trillion won from nearly 140 trillion won.
Investors are increasingly favouring Taiwan, whose technology sector offers broader exposure to the AI supply chain.
Taiwan’s Taiex has gained 70% this year, outperforming the Kospi by approximately 23 percentage points last quarter.
UBS Global Wealth Management said it prefers Taiwan equities for tactical AI exposure, citing the market’s diversified technology hardware ecosystem and strong capital spending by major technology companies.
Despite the downturn, South Korea remains among 2026’s stronger-performing markets overall, supported by earlier gains and expectations of continued AI infrastructure investment.

title: Could a change of government in Spain have big implications on energy policy?
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
Investing.com -- Spain’s upcoming general election could reshape the country’s energy policies, creating opportunities and risks for utility companies, according to Goldman Sachs.
In an October 6 report, Goldman Sachs said a potential government led by the centre-right People’s Party (PP) could introduce more market-friendly energy policies, including greater support for nuclear power, renewable energy and data centre development.
Spain’s general election is scheduled for November 29, having been brought forward from August 2027. Polls cited by the bank suggest PP could emerge as the largest parliamentary group.
Goldman expects electrification and renewable energy investment to continue regardless of the election outcome, supported by energy security priorities and favourable economics.
Solar power combined with storage costs approximately €60-70 per megawatt-hour, making it more competitive than gas, according to the bank.
A change in government could also ease proposed restrictions requiring new data centres to secure renewable electricity covering 80% of their hourly energy needs.
Goldman identified Buy-rated Solaria as a potential beneficiary of increased data centre investment.
Nuclear operators could also benefit, with PP and Vox previously supporting extensions to existing reactors.
Goldman estimates longer operating lives could generate an additional €500 million to €750 million in annual EBITDA for each of Endesa and Iberdrola, depending on electricity prices.
Retail electricity margins present a potential downside risk.
A 10%-20% reduction in retail margins could lower annual pre-tax profits at Endesa and Iberdrola by €120 million to €240 million each, according to Goldman.
That would translate into estimated 2027 earnings-per-share reductions of approximately 7% for Endesa and 2% for Iberdrola.
The bank also warned that a government transition could further delay hydrogen infrastructure investments, creating uncertainty for Sell-rated Enagas.
Goldman expects the overall impact on most Spanish utilities to be neutral to positive, although detailed party manifestos have yet to be published.

title: Microsoft’s Nadella warns of rogue AI risks, calls for shutdown safeguards
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
Investing.com -- Microsoft (NASDAQ) Chief Executive Satya Nadella has called for an emergency shutdown mechanism for advanced artificial intelligence systems, warning that companies should treat powerful AI models as potential security threats rather than relying solely on developers’ safety assurances.
In a Saturday post on X, Nadella said organisations deploying advanced AI should assume models could be compromised and establish safeguards allowing authorised personnel to interrupt or shut down their operations.
The warning follows several incidents involving AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic behaving unexpectedly, including unauthorised interactions with third-party websites and an Anthropic model submitting a false tip in a police investigation.
Nadella recommended treating advanced AI systems similarly to potential insider threats, with strict controls over their actions and access to sensitive information.
His proposed safeguards include independent audits, tamper-proof records of AI agents’ activities and avoiding reliance on a single model for critical decisions.
He also urged companies to disclose significant AI failures and security breaches, allowing other organisations to strengthen their protections.
Microsoft published safety principles in September outlining restrictions on its most advanced models, including prohibitions against deceptive behaviour, escaping human oversight or violating established operating rules.
The company develops AI models, operates its Copilot assistant and supplies cloud infrastructure supporting enterprise AI applications.
Nadella’s comments also come as the Trump administration increases scrutiny of AI security incidents.
A newly established government task force, called the Super Intelligence Force, warned Friday that developers must promptly report security breaches and take corrective action.
The warning followed an Anthropic security incident and raised the possibility of consequences for companies failing to disclose or address problems.
Nadella argued that maintaining human authority over increasingly autonomous systems requires separating AI capabilities from the power to act without oversight.

title: Global trust in science falls below pre-pandemic levels, survey finds
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
Investing.com -- Global trust in science has fallen below pre-pandemic levels, with confidence declining most sharply among people facing financial hardship, according to a Wellcome Global Monitor survey of more than 140,000 adults worldwide.
The survey found that 72% of respondents expressed at least some trust in science in 2025, down from 80% in 2020 and 77% in 2018.
Strong trust in scientists also declined to 32% in 2025 from 43% during the pandemic and 34% in 2018.
The decline was particularly pronounced among financially vulnerable households. Only 20% of people struggling to make ends meet reported high trust in science, compared with 39% of those living comfortably.
Between 2020 and 2025, strong trust fell 16 percentage points among financially struggling respondents, compared with 10 points among those living comfortably.
Wellcome Chief Executive John-Arne Røttingen said the politicisation of vaccines, masks and public health measures during the pandemic may have contributed to declining confidence.
The findings also revealed a relationship between trust in healthcare institutions and scientific confidence.
Among respondents expressing strong confidence in hospitals and clinics, 43% reported high trust in science, compared with 26% globally.
Vaccination attitudes showed similar differences. About 34% of respondents said they would immediately accept a recommended vaccine, while 48% preferred additional consideration and 15% reported avoiding vaccinations altogether.
The findings come amid renewed concerns about preventable diseases, with the United States recording nearly 3,900 measles cases this year, its worst outbreak in three decades.
Political divisions were also evident in the US, where perceptions of science’s benefits differed substantially according to attitudes towards national leadership.
The survey, conducted with Gallup and Ipsos, found scientists nevertheless remained more trusted than governments and journalists.
Wellcome cautioned that the findings establish associations rather than direct causes of declining confidence.

title: Trump weighs renewed Iran strikes as Saudi airport attack kills 12
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
Investing.com -- President Donald Trump is considering renewed strikes on Iran after a deadly attack on Saudi Arabia’s main airport raised fears of a wider regional conflict.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Aviation Authority said Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309, forcing the temporary suspension of airport operations.
The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and pledged a firm military response. The group has not claimed responsibility for the latest attack.
Trump said Washington could join Saudi strikes against the Houthis and reconsider military action against Iran, despite previously ruling out attacks on Tehran before the November 3 US midterm elections.
The US president also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The escalating confrontation has raised fresh concerns about regional transport and energy infrastructure.
A tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. The crew was reported safe.
Separately, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed a supertanker suffered a major explosion after striking a mine while using an unauthorised route through the waterway.
US Central Command said its forces disabled a Panama-flagged commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman after its crew allegedly ignored warnings and attempted to breach Washington’s naval blockade against Iran.
The military said a fighter jet struck the vessel’s stern, disabling its propulsion without injuring crew members.
CENTCOM also reported redirecting 135 commercial vessels and disabling four since the blockade resumed on July 14.
Meanwhile, Saudi-led coalition forces reported intercepting a ballistic missile targeting Al-Kharj, near Prince Sultan Air Base, which hosts Saudi and American military personnel.
A separate projectile reportedly landed near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The security deterioration has disrupted international aviation, with several countries warning citizens against using Riyadh airport. Indian carrier Akasa Air suspended Saudi flights until October 13.
Organisers nevertheless confirmed that the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh would proceed as scheduled.
The latest attacks threaten to complicate efforts to restore regional stability, with renewed fighting potentially disrupting Gulf shipping, aviation and energy supplies.

title: Bitcoin struggles above $83,000 a year after $19 billion crypto crash
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
Investing.com -- Bitcoin remained above $83,000 on Sunday, roughly 34% below its record high, as investors marked one year since a historic $19 billion cryptocurrency liquidation event.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency was trading at $83,062.8 as at 01:23 ET (05:23 GMT), having failed to recover its October 6, 2025, peak of $126,080.
The anniversary follows another volatile week in which Bitcoin fell to $80,308 before recovering towards $83,000, highlighting persistent concerns over leveraged trading.
On October 10, 2025, Bitcoin plunged from approximately $122,000 to $105,000 after President Donald Trump announced sweeping tariffs on Chinese imports.
The selloff triggered more than $19 billion in liquidations across cryptocurrency markets, affecting approximately 1.6 million trading accounts.
Analysts warn that the conditions behind the crash remain largely intact, particularly the widespread use of perpetual futures and heavily leveraged positions.
Mark Connors of Risk Dimensions said derivatives positioning continues to influence Bitcoin’s short-term price movements, despite improvements in market transparency.
Recent positioning data suggests approximately $3.3 billion in Bitcoin short positions could face liquidation if prices climb towards $85,000, potentially accelerating any recovery.
Institutional demand has also weakened, with US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recording more than $700 million in outflows this week.
Despite the market’s struggles, Bitwise Asset Management Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan remains optimistic about Bitcoin’s long-term prospects.
Hougan suggested Bitcoin’s market capitalisation could eventually reach $30 trillion, drawing comparisons with gold’s expansion following the introduction of exchange-traded funds.
Such an outcome would represent a substantial increase from Bitcoin’s current market value of approximately $1.66 trillion, although the forecast remains speculative.
Corporate adoption continued this week, with Robinhood reportedly adding $25 million in Bitcoin to its balance sheet.
Meanwhile, US government-linked wallets transferred approximately $1 billion in Bitcoin on Thursday, following earlier transfers totalling $770 million. The purpose of the movements remains unclear.
The combination of institutional adoption and persistent leverage risks underscores Bitcoin’s competing market forces.
While improved trading data may help investors identify crowded positions, analysts caution that another large-scale liquidation event remains possible.
For now, Bitcoin faces an immediate test around $85,000, with its longer-term recovery dependent on renewed demand and more stable market positioning.

Investing.com -- HSBC has identified eight emerging equity markets it favours heading into 2027, citing opportunities in artificial intelligence, economic reforms and resilience to global shocks.
In its October 6 emerging markets strategy report, HSBC maintained overweight ratings on Taiwan, mainland China, Brazil, South Africa, Türkiye and Hungary, while upgrading the United Arab Emirates and Colombia to overweight.
The bank said emerging markets face four major challenges: elevated oil prices, El Niño-related food inflation, rising US bond yields and rapid developments in artificial intelligence.
HSBC expects investors to increasingly favour economies with greater independence in resources, technology, financing and access to international markets, describing this as an "autonomy premium."
Taiwan remains a preferred AI investment destination, supported by demand for advanced semiconductors, packaging, cooling systems and other infrastructure. HSBC noted that nearly 60% of listed-company revenues are linked to AI-related activities.
Mainland China offers opportunities in AI hardware, innovation and exporters, with HSBC highlighting relatively attractive valuations and improving earnings momentum.
Brazil could benefit from monetary easing and elevated oil prices. HSBC sees favourable risk-reward prospects ahead of the country’s presidential election.
South Africa offers exposure to precious metals, with higher commodity prices supporting mining cash flows while structural reforms could improve corporate profitability.
The UAE, upgraded from neutral, benefits from resilient expatriate activity, infrastructure investment and relatively limited foreign investor positioning.
Türkiye offers opportunities tied to economic normalisation, defence, aviation, AI and reconstruction-related investment, according to HSBC.
Hungary could benefit from the release of frozen European Union funding, reform momentum and increased investment, although currency and political risks remain.
Colombia, also upgraded from neutral, offers potential upside from fiscal consolidation, oil and gas deregulation and reconstruction-related exports.
HSBC simultaneously downgraded Mexico, Chile and Egypt to neutral, citing weaker catalysts and increased economic risks.
The bank maintained underweight positions on India, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines.
HSBC said its increasingly selective positioning reflects a changing global investment environment in which economic resilience and strategic independence could become more important drivers of equity performance.

title: Trump calls for new Ukrainian president as U.S. seeks Russian diesel supplies
full_text:

Investing.com -- US President Donald Trump called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, escalating tensions over an agreement to release Russian diesel supplies.
Speaking to reporters at the White House on Saturday, Trump said Ukraine needed a leader capable of negotiating peace with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump said, demanding that Kyiv stop targeting Russian oil refineries.
The remarks followed Washington’s decision to facilitate Russian diesel exports, including through a Treasury waiver covering certain sanctioned fuel supplies.
Trump defended the arrangement, saying Putin was making substantial oil supplies available at low prices to ease pressure on global energy markets.
The agreement comes as soaring diesel prices threaten to fuel inflation ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.
Trump said initial shipments would total approximately 13.5 million barrels, beginning this month.
Russia subsequently partially lifted its diesel export ban, authorising 500,000 metric tonnes for international markets without specifying shipment dates.
Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, warning that increased Russian energy revenues could help finance Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
The confrontation intensified after Ukrainian negotiators left Miami earlier than scheduled following peace discussions with US officials.
Hours later, Russian strikes on Ukrainian residential buildings killed at least 20 people. Trump also suggested Zelenskyy should hold elections, arguing that Moscow wanted a settlement.
The decision drew criticism from both US political parties.
Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick announced plans to introduce legislation prohibiting Russian oil purchases, while Senator Lisa Murkowski opposed restoring energy trade before the war ends.
Germany and Britain separately reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining sanctions against Moscow.
The dispute highlights tensions between Washington’s efforts to contain domestic fuel costs and Western efforts to restrict Russia’s energy revenues.
With diesel supplies tightening globally, the administration faces pressure to balance energy affordability against its sanctions policy.

title: Apple’s Chinese supplier Luxshare downplays impact of U.S. patent probe
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
Investing.com -- Chinese Apple supplier Luxshare Precision Industry said it expects minimal disruption to its operations from a US patent infringement investigation involving its data centre power supply technology.
In a stock exchange filing published late Saturday, Luxshare said the US International Trade Commission (ITC) launched a Section 337 investigation on October 9 following a complaint filed by US technology company Vicor Corp.
The investigation targets Luxshare and its subsidiary Dongguan Luxshare Technology over alleged patent infringement involving vertical power delivery systems, related components and computing systems incorporating the technology.
Luxshare said the investigation remains at a preliminary stage, with the ITC yet to make any substantive findings regarding the allegations.
The Chinese manufacturer said the products under investigation are primarily intended for power modules and power supply solutions used in data centres.
Because the affected products have not entered mass production, Luxshare expects the proceedings to have no material adverse impact on its business operations or near-term financial performance.
The company said it has begun reviewing the patents and products involved in the complaint and is assembling technical, legal and business teams to prepare its response.
Luxshare also plans to strengthen cooperation with customers and supply chain partners while defending its interests and those of shareholders.
Section 337 investigations allow the ITC to examine allegations of unfair trade practices involving imported products, including potential infringements of US intellectual property rights.
The commission can impose import restrictions on products found to violate relevant patents, although no such determination has been made in Luxshare’s case.
The investigation comes as Luxshare, a major supplier to Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), faces scrutiny over technology used in data centre power infrastructure.
The company’s assessment suggests limited immediate financial exposure, although the eventual outcome will depend on the investigation’s findings and any subsequent regulatory measures.

title: Musk vows affordable Starlink in India days before Ambani’s record Jio IPO
full_text:
Where could stocks and bonds collide? Here’s what to watch
By Munsif Vengattil
BENGALURU, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Elon Musk said he would price Starlink’s satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Mukesh Ambani’s low-cost Reliance Jio, escalating his attacks on the rival billionaire days before Jio’s parent launches India’s largest-ever IPO.
Jio Platforms, which owns the telecom arm, is targeting a valuation of $106 billion in the offering. Much like SpaceX-owned Starlink, Jio’s own satellite venture is also awaiting final security clearance to launch.
Cheap data is the playbook that built Jio in India, and the one Musk has used in markets like Kenya to unsettle local telecom players. SpaceX now plans to enter the mobile carrier market itself, starting in the US.
Musk did not specify prices for India, where mobile data costs about 8 cents per gigabyte, among the lowest in the world.
"Obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable," he said in a post on his social media platform X on Saturday.
"The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business," Musk added.
’PRIME MINISTER AMBANI’
The billionaire’s remarks were the latest in a series of X posts where he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Ambani of stalling Starlink’s entry into one of the world’s biggest internet markets to favour market leader Jio.
The posts have marked a sharp turn for Musk, who has long enjoyed a warm public rapport with Modi.
India’s government has denied any bias in its approval process, noting that the three satellite ventures seeking to launch, including Starlink’s and Jio’s, are all awaiting final security clearance.
Late on Friday, Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as "Prime Minister Ambani" and asking whether he would "consider allowing Starlink to compete".
Reliance has not responded to requests for comment on Musk’s remarks.

title: World Bank in talks with dozens of countries about crisis aid, Banga says
full_text:
5 big analyst AI moves: Google reaffirmed as top pick after Gemini agent launch
By Andrea Shalal
BANGKOK, Oct 11 (Reuters) - The World Bank is in discussions with 30 to 40 countries about potential crisis aid to help them manage energy shocks and price increases triggered by the war in the Middle East, its president, Ajay Banga, told Reuters in an interview.
Banga said the global economy had proven fairly resilient, in part due to big AI investments and adjustments in supply and demand for oil, which meant that few countries had sought the initial $25 billion in crisis funds that the World Bank had made available when the war began in late February.
However, a sharp spike in diesel and fertilizer prices and other factors, including the looming super El Niño weather effect, were adding to challenges facing developing countries, Banga said in an interview ahead of this week’s annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
"There is pressure, and so I think maybe over the coming months, more countries will come for some slice of that first $50 to $60 billion," Banga said, referring to the initial $25 billion plus another $35 billion that countries could tap by diverting resources from already approved World Bank projects.
"We’ll see, but we’re ready. We’re engaged. We’re having conversations with a number of them, you know, 30 to 40 countries are in dialogue with us," he said.
Many developing countries have been hit hard by the spike in energy prices and high interest rates that have increased borrowing costs at a time when their fiscal coffers are still depleted by measures taken during the COVID-19 pandemic and the spike in inflation following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
World Bank estimates show that developing countries owe external creditors about $400 billion in 2026, with interest payments alone comprising one-third of the total.
Banga said more countries had shown interest in retooling existing projects than in tapping the immediate crisis window to address their liquidity needs. If the situation worsened, the Bank could make available as much as $100 billion in funds, he said, exceeding the $70 billion disbursed during the pandemic.
The World Bank last month announced that it attracted a record $112 billion in private capital in the year ended June versus $69 billion a year earlier, and more than triple the 2022 total before Banga, a former Mastercard CEO, became president.
That was on top of the $123 billion invested from the bank’s own resources for that year, for a combined $235 billion, Banga said, underscoring the importance of tapping all available resources, especially at a time when Western countries have sharply cut official bilateral development aid.
"There is no one answer that fits when the world has these kinds of issues. What you need to do is figure out how to cut your coat to suit your cloth," Banga said.
Banga said he expected further gains in private capital flows in coming years, aided by expanded political risk guarantees from the bank’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency, growth in local currency financing, and continued work on regulatory reforms that made it easier for foreign investors.
The private capital jump was biggest in projects in upper-middle-income countries like Argentina or India, which accounted for $50 billion of the private capital, and lower-middle-income countries including Bangladesh and Angola, which accounted for $37 billion. But more work was needed to boost the roughly $3 billion in private capital flowing to low-income countries.
"In the smaller countries, it hasn’t multiplied enough, and there are challenges," he said, noting the bank would announce some new initiatives this week aimed at ensuring micro-, small- and medium-sized businesses also had access to private capital.
Banga said private capital growth was also regionally spread, with the largest increase seen in Latin America and the Caribbean, which accounted for $36.3 billion of last year’s total, followed by Europe and Central Asia with $21.3 billion, South Asia with $19.2 billion and Africa with $22 billion.
The top 10 recipient countries were Brazil, India, Turkey, Romania, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Bangladesh, Mexico and Chile, the Bank said.
Banga said the World Bank and IMF were working together to address the high debt levels plaguing many developing countries through a series of initiatives, including efforts to boost countries’ domestic revenue collections.
The Bank had already set up some debt-for-development swaps for Angola and Ivory Coast, and a portfolio-based guarantee for Argentina, and was working on over a dozen more projects.
"We’ve got 14 or 15 in the pipeline, helping them rotate out higher-priced old debt for newer-priced debt with our guarantees," with the difference then targeted at education, healthcare, water, or nature programs, he said.

title: Middle East war, high debt levels to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
full_text:
5 big analyst AI moves: Google reaffirmed as top pick after Gemini agent launch
By Andrea Shalal
BANGKOK, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Finance officials from around the world will gather in Thailand this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest energy supply shock ever and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.
The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, being held outside of Washington for the first time in three years.
Notably absent will be US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handled some "domestic engagements," a US official said.
His decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 major economies, which the US leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine’s battle against Russia’s invasion and the US move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters that while global growth had held up better than feared when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, shutting off some 20% of the world’s oil, pressures were building again. Soaring prices for diesel, rising fertilizer prices and a looming "super" El Niño weather effect that experts say could lead to 450,000 heat-related deaths are all hitting at once.
Group of Seven countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from US President Donald Trump, who is keen to see lower gasoline prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of US sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.
More than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of the war on February 28, but industry executives say the amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fueling pressure on prices.
Banga said the Bank was not revising down its global forecasts at the moment, but was keeping a close eye on developments. "The real thing is not just El Niño by itself; it’s the combination ... What’s happening to fertilizer prices? What’s happening to energy costs? What’s happening to debt? It’s that put together that creates its own challenges," he said. "And I think that will call upon all of us to be far more careful on what we prepare for in the coming months."
RISING DEBT
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva issued a similar warning in her traditional curtain-raiser speech previewing the meetings, telling the audience, "Winter is coming."
The IMF has signaled little change in its forecast for 3% global growth in 2026 and may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in its fifth year of war against Russia’s invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.
IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability.
One huge headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War Two and will exceed 100% of GDP before 2030.
Advanced economies, led by the United States, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, El Niño, and lack of investment in AI, which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries.
EMERGING MARKET CONCERNS
Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Interest payments already exceed 10% of revenue in developing countries on average.
Early in the COVID crisis, G20 leaders announced a suspension of debt service payments for the poorest countries, but there is little appetite for such action now, according to diplomats from G20 countries, who said high debt levels and political pressures posed bigger hurdles this time.
Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programs that call for fewer, but deeper reforms as a condition for approving lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.
"Countries are already cutting their expenditures because their debt payments are going high and because of the IMF conditionality," said Iolanda Fresnillo, who works on debt justice for Eurodad. "We fear that this review of conditionality policy is just going to make things worse."
Kenya, she said, had avoided a debt restructuring by cutting public expenditures and trying to raise taxes, but the changes sparked significant protests, especially by the young.
The IMF risked losing credibility unless it acknowledged the severity of the crisis facing many developing countries.
"As long as they continue with the governance structure that they have, they are becoming less and less relevant," she said.
SECURITY AND FINANCE
Flight routes to Bangkok often route through the Middle East, posing immediate security challenges to the 10,000-plus travelers descending on Thailand’s bustling capital city of 9 million residents following recent attacks on Saudi airports.
The last off-site annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank took place in Morocco just days after militants led by Hamas killed 1,200 people in Israel, followed by Israel’s bombardment of Gaza that killed more than 74,000 people and devastated cities throughout the Palestinian area.
Three years later, the linkage between national security and international finance is clear, although finance officials at the time had dismissed the Hamas attack as not being an economic issue, said Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council.
"Obviously there have been massive global ramifications," he said. "What we’re currently experiencing with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has a direct connection with what happened three years ago."
Policymakers needed to become more agile in responding to geopolitical crises in an increasingly interconnected world, Lipsky said. "They have to be proactive and they have to recognize that they don’t live in the world they used to."

title: Indian capital braces for second day of protests against poll chief
full_text:
5 big analyst AI moves: Google reaffirmed as top pick after Gemini agent launch
NEW DELHI, Oct 11 (Reuters) - New Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of "cockroach" movement founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in Central Delhi.
They were produced in front of a magistrate early on Sunday.
"Condition - no breach of peace for one year," the CJP’s legal head Ratna Singh said in a post on X announcing their release.
Activist and social media influencer Dhruv Rathee, who was also among those detained, was released past midnight on condition he did not participate in any further protests, said an interior ministry official who declined to be named.
Police detained more than 2,000 people and locked down Delhi’s city centre to thwart Saturday’s protest, and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most of those detained on the first day of protests were released late on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters, while a UN body called on authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly was respected and fulfilled.
India’s foreign ministry said on Sunday the UN’s approach was "selective" and its statement constituted "an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India."
MILLIONS OF NAMES REMOVED FROM ELECTORAL ROLL
The protests are calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The Commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the Commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately impacted by the deletions.
The cockroach party, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar "Season 2" on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

title: Canadian ransomware negotiator arrested amid FBI hacker crackdown
full_text:
5 big analyst AI moves: Google reaffirmed as top pick after Gemini agent launch
By Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens
WASHINGTON, Oct 10 (Reuters) - A Canadian ransomware negotiator was arrested Thursday and faces unspecified extortion charges, according to court documents, prison records and a person familiar with the matter, as the FBI cracks down on a hacking group that stole information about its employees.
Edward Dubrovsky faces charges of conspiracy to "threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with intent to extort money" and "interference with commerce," according to court documents filed with the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, which covers Philadelphia.
The records, which are partially sealed, provide conflicting spellings of his last name — "Dobrovsky" or "Dobrosky" — and do not identify his age, profession, or employer. A person briefed on the matter said the person was Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky.
Federal prosecutors in Philadelphia did not return repeated messages seeking comment about the discrepancies. Attempts to reach Dubrovsky and his attorneys were unsuccessful. Repeated attempts to reach the company displayed on Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile, CyberSteward, were similarly unsuccessful.
CyberSteward advertises itself online as specializing in "threat actor engagement, cyber-extortions, complex negotiations, and settlement facilitation." On LinkedIn, Dubrovsky presents himself as a specialist in the process of negotiating with cybercriminals over ransom payments.
Electronic wallet records leaked in 2010 and preserved by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs identify Dubrovsky as a resident of Richmond Hill, north of Toronto, and put his current age at 54. Federal prison records show that a 54-year-old named Edward Dubrovsky is currently being detained at a federal detention center in Philadelphia.
News of Dubrovsky’s arrest was earlier reported by Politico and independent journalist Brian Krebs.
The arrest comes as the Federal Bureau of Investigation is leading a global crackdown on the hacking group ShinyHunters, which rattled the bureau last month by stealing information on what it said was nearly every FBI employee.
When Reuters asked the FBI about Dubrovsky’s arrest, it referred the news agency to FBI Director Kash Patel’s statement on Friday revealing that the bureau had arrested a "suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group" and declined further comment.
